I Want Your Sex

✅ NOT A WOKE TRAP

I Want Your Sex is not a woke trap. The sexual content, BDSM power dynamics, and rejection of traditional relationship norms are evident from the first act. Erika initiates a dominant-submissive sexual relationship with Elliot during his first week working for her. The film announces its intentions immediately and sustains them throughout the 90-minute runtime. Nothing is hidden past the halfway mark. Viewers who buy a ticket for a Gregg Araki erotic thriller titled 'I Want Your Sex' know what they are getting before the lights go down.

Our Verdict on I Want Your Sex

Gregg Araki has been making films about sex, power, and queer identity for over thirty years. I Want Your Sex is being called his most accessible work yet. By Araki standards, that is true. By any other standard, this is still a film in which a young man is handcuffed to a corner while his boss attempts to persuade his female best friend to peg him with a strap-on. Accessibility is relative.

The film stars Olivia Wilde as Erika Tracy, a renowned contemporary artist whose work is sexually explicit, confrontational, and commercially successful within the rarefied world of gallery openings and seven-figure sales. Cooper Hoffman, in his first major role since Licorice Pizza, plays Elliot, an unemployed twenty-something who becomes Erika's studio assistant and, almost immediately, her submissive sexual partner. The dynamic is established with remarkable speed: by the end of Elliot's first week, Erika has summoned him to her office and instructed him to crawl to her. He does. The BDSM power exchange that follows is the film's central relationship, and everything else orbits it.

Wilde is genuinely good here. Erika is controlling, magnetic, and unknowable in a way that serves the film's thriller ambitions. She is not a cartoon dominatrix but a woman who has weaponized desire into a career and an identity. Hoffman's Elliot is less fully realized. He is reactive by design, a character to whom things happen rather than someone who makes things happen. This is the point: Elliot is the submissive, the canvas Erika paints on. But a protagonist without clear agency for ninety minutes tests the audience's investment, particularly once the film asks us to care whether he escapes Erika's orbit.

The supporting cast does solid work. Mason Gooding is warm and grounded as Zap, Elliot's co-worker and eventual roommate, providing the film's only genuine friendship. Chase Sui Wonders plays Apple, Elliot's best friend, with a kind of desperate sincerity that makes the pegging scene land as genuinely uncomfortable rather than comic. Daveed Diggs brings professional menace as Vikktor, Erika's business manager. Charli XCX, in her film debut, has limited screen time as Elliot's disinterested girlfriend Minerva but makes an impression: she communicates more about the character's indifference to Elliot in thirty seconds of screen time than most pop-star-turned-actors manage in entire films.

The plot pivots around a mid-film twist: Erika and Vikktor have been manipulating Elliot from the start, drugging his champagne and faking Erika's death to generate publicity for her gallery exhibition. The hoax works. The show sells out. Elliot, having been publicly humiliated at the gallery and privately violated through the staged death, is told by Erika that he should use the scandal to boost his own career. He does. Two years later, he is a successful podcaster interviewing Erika about the book she wrote chronicling the hoax. The film's final reveal, a shared nightmare in which Elliot and Erika's wedding dissolves into body horror, suggests that neither of them has escaped the other. It is a clever ending that does not fully earn its cleverness.

From the VirtueVigil perspective, I Want Your Sex is not a complicated call. The film is built on the premise that sexual submission to a dominant older woman is a form of liberation for a young man. Elliot's refusals, his discomfort with the strap-on, his desire for monogamous connection, are all framed as deficiencies he needs to overcome. The film does not quite say that traditional male sexuality is toxic, but it comes close enough that the distinction is academic. The pegging scene is the clearest example: Elliot's adamant refusal is presented as the moment he fails the film's sexual test, and Apple's tearful response frames his refusal as a rejection of her rather than a legitimate boundary. The film's moral universe does not include the possibility that a man might decline to be penetrated and be right to do so.

The satire of the contemporary art world is the film's most broadly enjoyable element, and it is satisfying in the way all art-world satire is: empty gallery openings, pretentious patrons, commerce dressed as transcendence. But even this satire serves the film's progressive thesis: Erika's exploitation of Elliot through emotionally abusive means is presented with a wink, as though her bad behavior is redeemed by her artistic seriousness and her status as a woman in a male-dominated art world. The film wants to critique the art market without fully condemning the artist who manipulates it.

I Want Your Sex is a well-made film by a director who knows exactly what he is doing. It is well-acted, stylishly shot, and tightly paced at ninety minutes. Whether it is enjoyable depends entirely on your tolerance for explicit BDSM content and your willingness to accept the film's central premise that sexual liberation requires the demolition of traditional boundaries. If you bring that willingness, you will find a sharp, funny, occasionally unsettling erotic thriller. If you do not, you will find ninety minutes of provocation that mistakes transgression for insight.

Creative Team Deep Dive

Director: Gregg Araki

STRONGLY PROGRESSIVE. Araki is one of the defining voices of New Queer Cinema, a movement that emerged in the early 1990s to center LGBTQ narratives and aesthetics in independent film. His body of work from The Living End (1992) through Mysterious Skin (2004), Kaboom (2010), and the Starz series Now Apocalypse (2019) has been consistently and explicitly about sexual identity, queer desire, and the rejection of heteronormative constraints. Araki does not make traditional films. He does not pretend to. I Want Your Sex, despite being marketed as his most accessible work, is a continuation of the same thematic project he has pursued for over three decades. He is among the most ideologically consistent directors working in American independent cinema.

Gregg Araki earned his MFA from USC's School of Cinematic Arts and emerged as part of the New Queer Cinema movement with The Living End (1992), an HIV-themed road movie that established his voice: confrontational, sexually explicit, formally adventurous, and politically engaged. His most acclaimed film remains Mysterious Skin (2004), starring a young Joseph Gordon-Levitt as a gay prostitute processing childhood sexual abuse. Araki's work consistently explores sexual identity, trauma, power, and the boundaries of desire. White Bird in a Blizzard (2014) was his most mainstream effort before I Want Your Sex. Kaboom (2010) won the first Queer Palm at Cannes. He has never made a film that could be described as ideologically traditional, and I Want Your Sex does not break that streak.

Content Breakdown

Adult Viewer Insight

I Want Your Sex makes an argument about sexual freedom that deserves to be taken seriously because it is made with genuine craft. The argument is this: traditional sexual boundaries, monogamy, male sexual agency, and the refusal to participate in BDSM power exchange are limitations imposed by an unexamined culture rather than legitimate expressions of personal preference or moral conviction. Elliot's arc is structured as an awakening, with each boundary he crosses presented as growth. The film's sophistication makes this argument more persuasive than it would be coming from a lesser filmmaker. Araki knows how to make transgression feel like liberation rather than destruction. The question the film does not ask is whether liberation from all boundaries is actually freedom or merely a different kind of captivity. Elliot ends the film financially successful and professionally secure, but the shared nightmare suggests he is as trapped by Erika as he ever was. The film's final image, two people waking from the same nightmare in separate beds, is more honest than the preceding eighty-nine minutes. It acknowledges, perhaps despite itself, that what the film has been selling as liberation may be a different arrangement of the same furniture.

Parental Guidance

Rated R for strong sexual content including explicit BDSM depictions, full nudity, strong language, and drug use. I Want Your Sex is an adults-only film. The sexual content is not simulated or obscured. Parents should not consider this for viewers under 18, and many adult viewers will find the content challenging. The film depicts a sexual relationship built on power exchange and manipulation. The pegging sequence is genuinely uncomfortable and not played for comedy. Conservative families: this is not your film.
